events.title: Estonian youths offer arson and property damage services online

articles.text: News Kristjan Pihl, Irina Kablukova {{1793864520000 | amCalendar}} share Facebook X (Twitter) e-mail Burnt Mercedes-Benz passenger car. Source: Screenshot from "Pealtnägija" News Russia is stepping up its campaign of arson and sabotage across Europe, increasingly recruiting petty criminals through social media to carry out attacks that test the limits of Western tolerance and risk causing mass casualties, Estonian security experts warn. Almost every day brings news of hybrid attacks in Europe. Russia, in particular, is constantly testing how far it can go before its actions can be classified as a direct military attack. One increasingly common form of such attacks is arson, as illustrated by the fire at Milrem Robotics' factory in Lasnamäe. Rather than trained James Bond-style operatives, the perpetrators are often local petty criminals. "I got home with my friends at around 11 p.m. We had dinner, chatted and went to bed. I hadn't even fallen asleep when I heard some unusual noise outside. I looked out the window and saw that the car parked next to my house was already on fire," recalled Ruslan, a victim of a series of arson attacks. The 50-year-old small-business owner from Harju County has been the target of a criminal campaign and his life and property may still be at risk. Over the past three years, at least four passenger cars he used have caught fire, along with a vacation cabin, while a building he owned that operated as a tourist center burned to the ground. "Absolutely every time, without exception, there were people either in adjacent rooms or in the immediate vicinity. The greatest distance between the fire and the people was 10 meters," Ruslan added. The repeated fires involving his property are remarkable in themselves, but it has since emerged that Ruslan's attackers were also carrying out an assignment for Russian military intelligence during the same period. Russia has been organizing similar acts of vandalism and arson across Europe at an accelerating pace, with the aim, according to experts, of sowing confusion and testing how far it can go before its actions are considered overt aggression. "Looking at the potentially bloody operations they have undertaken in the past, you could say they have calculated that there could be a major explosion and they still wouldn't face a serious response," security expert Meelis Oidsalu explained. "These attacks have become increasingly dangerous: Explosives are being used and buildings are being set on fire. We also know of cases in Europe where individuals have been targeted. These are all quite serious activities and I would say that the more desperate Russia becomes in its war in Ukraine, the more intense these attacks could become," said Marta Tuul, bureau chief of the Estonian Internal Security Service (ISS/KAPO). To be clear, Ruslan is not a GRU target. The motive behind the attacks against him is personal and the investigation into who is seeking revenge against him is still ongoing. Nevertheless, Ruslan's case provides a vivid illustration of how a series of arson attacks is carried out. "Because things kept happening to me systematically that were difficult to anticipate and that I couldn't understand, I was forced to install cameras. I installed video surveillance everywhere, incidentally, on the police's recommendation," Ruslan said. On October 31 last year, a few minutes after midnight, two hooded men approached the gate of Ruslan's home just outside Tallinn. Both had their faces covered and one was carrying a canister. The men approached the car Ruslan used for work, doused it with gasoline and, moments later, flames erupted. Surprisingly, the arsonists did not stop there. Just an hour and a half later, at around 1:30 a.m., two apparently similar hooded figures arrived at Ruslan's summer property and attempted to set fire to a cabin there. However, either a mistake by the attackers or the damp weather prevented a larger fire. To Ruslan's surprise, the investigation was handed over to the ISS, with prosecutor Gardi Anderson, who has handled several other hybrid attack cases, taking charge of the proceedings. "At first, I was surprised, but later everything fell into place. The suspects are not only suspected of committing a crime against me, but also of offenses against public order and the state," Ruslan said. A few weeks after the latest arson attack, three young men from Maardu were detained: Martin Jaagumets, then 23, Aleksandr Grebeljuk, 22, and a 14-year-old boy whom we will identify only by the initial D because he is a minor. "In this particular case, we are dealing with three young men who are friends, come from the same place and share common interests," Anderson explained. "The young men were members of the same Telegram group where a job was posted calling for four arson attacks. Anyone in the group could have picked it up. This time, these young men decided to accept the assignment and announced that they would carry it out." A group called "МАШИНА," or "CAR," exists on the Telegram messaging app where, astonishingly, an advertisement was posted seeking people willing to carry out arson attacks. The three young men in our story took up the offer. The clients, using the aliases "Hardu" and "Said," provided a list of addresses and instructions to find a vehicle, buy lighter fluid, carry out the arson attacks, film the execution of the assignments and send video evidence. They were promised €1,000 for each job. Counterintelligence agencies in several countries confirm that trained agents are not used to carry out such acts. Instead, petty criminals and fools are recruited through social media. "Often, there are several links in this chain. Someone in the group notices a job offer and passes it on. In recent cases, we can say that the people accepting these offers are individuals who have had trouble in life. [...] When an offer is posted in a Telegram group, someone picks it up and passes it along. The vandals who are offered the jobs are often drug addicts, petty thieves or fraudsters. Sometimes the perpetrators know who they are working for and sometimes they don't," Tuul explained. The trio's campaign of destruction took place in late October last year. First, on the night of October 29–30, they set fire to a Mercedes-Benz parked in the courtyard of an apartment building in Lasnamäe while its owner was asleep at home. On the night of October 30–31, they set fire to Ruslan's car and vacation property. Then, on the night of October 31–November 1, they vandalized memorials to soldiers killed in the Battles of the Blue Hills in the village of Vaivara, Ida-Viru County. Investigators also obtained videos the young men had recorded and sent to their clients. The vandalized memorials in the Blue Hills (Sinimäed.)
